**Proof.**

Let $I = \{i_1, \ldots, i_k\}$ and let $J = \{1, \ldots, n\} \setminus I = \{j_1, \ldots, j_{n-k}\}$ (listed in increasing order). Set
$$E_I = \operatorname{span}(e_{i_1}, \ldots, e_{i_k}), \qquad E_J = \operatorname{span}(e_{j_1}, \ldots, e_{j_{n-k}}),$$
so $\mathbb{R}^n = E_I \oplus E_J$. Denote by $\pi_I : \mathbb{R}^n \to E_I$ the projection onto $E_I$ along $E_J$.

**Definition of the map.** For $V \in U_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}$, the restriction $\pi_I|_V : V \to E_I$ is a linear isomorphism by hypothesis. Hence for each $a \in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ there is a unique vector $v_a \in V$ satisfying $\pi_I(v_a) = e_{i_a}$. Since $\pi_I|_V$ is an isomorphism, the vectors $v_1, \ldots, v_k$ form a basis of $V$.

Decompose each $v_a$ according to $\mathbb{R}^n = E_I \oplus E_J$:
$$v_a = e_{i_a} + \sum_{b=1}^{n-k} x_{ba}\, e_{j_b}, \qquad x_{ba} \in \mathbb{R}.$$
Collect the coefficients into the matrix $X = (x_{ba}) \in \mathbb{R}^{(n-k)\times k}$ and define
$$f_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}(V) = X \in \mathbb{R}^{(n-k)\times k} \cong \mathbb{R}^{k(n-k)}.$$

**Well-definedness.** The vectors $v_a$ are uniquely determined by $V$ (because $\pi_I|_V$ is an isomorphism), so $X$ depends only on $V$, not on any auxiliary choices.

**Injectivity.** Suppose $f(V) = f(V') = X$. Then both $V$ and $V'$ are spanned by the same vectors $\{v_a\}_{a=1}^k$ with $v_a = e_{i_a} + \sum_b x_{ba} e_{j_b}$, so $V = V'$.

**Surjectivity.** Given any $X = (x_{ba}) \in \mathbb{R}^{(n-k)\times k}$, define
$$v_a = e_{i_a} + \sum_{b=1}^{n-k} x_{ba}\, e_{j_b}, \qquad a = 1, \ldots, k,$$
and set $V = \operatorname{span}(v_1, \ldots, v_k)$. The $E_I$-components of $v_1, \ldots, v_k$ are $e_{i_1}, \ldots, e_{i_k}$, which are linearly independent; hence $v_1, \ldots, v_k$ are linearly independent and $\dim V = k$. Moreover $\pi_I(v_a) = e_{i_a}$, so $\pi_I|_V$ sends a basis of $V$ to a basis of $E_I$ and is therefore an isomorphism. Thus $V \in U_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}$ and $f_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}(V) = X$.

**Continuity (both directions).** We topologize the Grassmannian $G(k,n)$ as the quotient of the space of full-rank $n \times k$ matrices
$$\mathcal{F} = \{B \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times k} : \operatorname{rank}(B) = k\}$$
by the equivalence relation $B \sim B'$ iff $\operatorname{col}(B) = \operatorname{col}(B')$, with quotient map $q: \mathcal{F} \to G(k,n)$.

For a matrix $B \in \mathcal{F}$, let $B_I \in \mathbb{R}^{k\times k}$ (resp. $B_J \in \mathbb{R}^{(n-k)\times k}$) be the submatrix of rows indexed by $I$ (resp. $J$). Then $q(B) \in U_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}$ iff $B_I$ is invertible. The preimage $q^{-1}(U_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}) = \{B \in \mathcal{F} : \det B_I \neq 0\}$ is open in $\mathcal{F}$, so $U_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}$ is open in $G(k,n)$.

*Continuity of $f$.* On $q^{-1}(U_{i_1,\ldots,i_k})$, the composition $f \circ q$ is given by
$$(f \circ q)(B) = B_J \, B_I^{-1}.$$
Indeed, the canonical representative of $V = q(B)$ is $B\, B_I^{-1}$, whose $I$-rows are $B_I B_I^{-1} = I_k$ and whose $J$-rows are $B_J B_I^{-1}$. Matrix inversion is continuous on the open set of invertible matrices, and matrix multiplication is continuous, so $f \circ q$ is continuous. Since $q$ is a quotient map (and its restriction to $q^{-1}(U_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}) \to U_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}$ is a quotient map onto the open set $U_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}$), the continuity of $f \circ q$ implies the continuity of $f$.

*Continuity of $f^{-1}$.* The inverse map sends $X \in \mathbb{R}^{(n-k)\times k}$ to the subspace $V = \operatorname{col}(M(X))$ where $M(X) \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ is the matrix with $I$-rows equal to $I_k$ and $J$-rows equal to $X$. The map $X \mapsto M(X)$ is continuous (it is an affine embedding of $\mathbb{R}^{(n-k)\times k}$ into $\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$), and $M(X)$ has full rank $k$ for all $X$ (its $I$-rows are $I_k$). Composing with the quotient map $q$ gives $f^{-1} = q \circ M$, which is continuous.

**Conclusion.** $f_{i_1,\ldots,i_k} : U_{i_1,\ldots,i_k} \to \mathbb{R}^{k(n-k)}$ is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, hence a homeomorphism. $\blacksquare$
